notes.title: Observation tools
notes.html:
On the ground: ASOS (automated airport stations), mesonets (dense local stations), buoys (water). Aloft: radiosondes on balloons, aircraft reports.

Radar productShows
ReflectivityHow much precipitation, and where
Base velocityMotion toward or away from the radar
Correlation coefficient (CC)How alike the targets are. Rain is high. Debris is low
Storm relative motionWinds with the storm's own movement removed. Shows rotation
Composite reflectivityStrongest echo at any height
Wind profileWinds at each height over the radar

Satellite: visible needs daylight. Infrared (IR) works day and night: cold cloud tops are bright, so tall storms stand out. Water vapor shows moisture in the middle and upper air.

Velocity: toward the radar is NEGATIVE (green). Away is POSITIVE (red). Think "red = run away".

notes.title: Station models and METAR
notes.html:
A station model packs temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and sky cover into one symbol.

SpotMeans
Upper leftTemperature
Lower leftDew point
Upper rightPressure, last 3 digits (tenths of mb)
Lower right3-hour pressure change
Center circleSky cover (more filled = cloudier)
Barb staffPoints toward where wind COMES FROM
Half flag / full / pennant5 kt / 10 kt / 50 kt
Pressure: 500 or more → put 9 in front. Less than 500 → put 10.132 → 1013.2 mb 987 → 998.7 mb 047 → 1004.7 mb

METAR example: KOKC 202153Z 18018G28KT 6SM TSRA BKN040CB 27/22 A2985

PartMeaning
KOKCStation
202153ZDay 20, 21:53 UTC
18018G28KTFrom 180° at 18 kt, gusts 28 kt
6SMVisibility 6 statute miles
TSRAThunderstorm with rain
BKN040CBBroken clouds at 4,000 ft, cumulonimbus
27/22Temp 27°C, dew point 22°C
A2985Altimeter 29.85 inHg

Sky: FEW 1–2/8, SCT 3–4/8, BKN 5–7/8, OVC 8/8. Height × 100 ft. Negative temps start with M (M05 = −5°C).

notes.title: Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
notes.html:
Standard levels: 850 mb (low moisture), 700 mb (steering), 500 mb (troughs and ridges), 300 mb (jet stream).

Hodograph: plots the wind at each height as a point, then connects them. A long, curving path means strong shear. Curving clockwise with height (veering) favors supercells.

Stüve / Skew-T: temperature (solid) and dew point (dashed) against pressure. Lines close together = moist or cloudy. Far apart = dry. A layer where temperature rises with height is an inversion (very stable, a "cap").

States/Nationals:

LCL (m) ≈ 125 × (T − Td in °C)Dry parcel cools 10 °C per km. Typical air cools about 6.5 °C per km.
CAPE (J/kg)Instability
Under 1,000Marginal
1,000–2,500Moderate
2,500–4,000Strong
Over 4,000Extreme
Low LCL (low cloud base) raises tornado risk. CAPE alone is not enough: you also need shear and a lift trigger.

notes.title: Setup for severe weather
notes.html:
Recipe: moisture + instability + lift + wind shear.

IngredientRole
Jet streamSteers storms, adds energy aloft
Cold frontCold air pushes in. Fast, sharp storms
Warm frontWarm air slides over cold. Wide, steady precipitation
StationaryStalled boundary
OccludedCold front catches warm front
DrylineMoisture boundary (moist east, dry west on the Plains). Not a temperature boundary
Atmospheric riverNarrow stream of heavy water vapor. Extreme rain at landfall
Wind shearWind changes with height. Organizes storms; directional shear starts rotation
FetchDistance wind blows over water
Ocean heat contentWarm deep water fuels hurricanes. Storm wakes are cooler

Mountains lift air (trigger storms), and can block, weaken or redirect storms.

notes.title: Severe-weather clouds
notes.html:
CloudSignal
CumulonimbusThe thunderstorm cloud
Wall cloudLowered, often rotating base under the updraft. Tornado warning sign
Shelf cloudWedge at the leading edge. Marks the gust front
Funnel cloudRotating cone not touching ground
MammatusPouches under an anvil. Often a storm weakening
Funnel cloud = not on the ground. Once it touches down it is a tornado.

notes.title: Drought and heat waves
notes.html:
Drought: long stretch with too little precipitation. Heat wave: long stretch of abnormal heat. Both are often caused by a blocking high-pressure ridge that sits in place and steers storms away.

Effects: crop loss, water limits, wildfire, heat illness, power demand.

notes.title: Precipitation, flooding, IDF
notes.html:
How it forms:

ProcessResult
Collision-coalescenceDrops merge into bigger drops (warm clouds)
Bergeron processIce crystals grow while supercooled drops shrink (cold clouds)
RimingSupercooled drops freeze onto ice (builds graupel and hail)
AggregationIce crystals stick together (snowflakes)
TypeLayers it fell through
SnowCold all the way down
SleetSnow melts, then refreezes as ice pellets in a cold layer near the ground
Freezing rainRain falls on a surface below 0 °C and freezes on contact
HailStrong updraft keeps stones aloft, they grow by riming
RainWarm all the way down

Flood types: flash (minutes to hours), stream/river (rises over days), urban (drains overwhelmed). Burn scars and steep land produce debris flows and mudslides.

Hail: pea ¼ in, penny ¾ in, quarter 1 in (severe), golf ball 1¾ in, baseball 2¾ in.

States/Nationals: an IDF curve shows rainfall intensity versus duration for a return period. Longer duration = lower intensity. Rarer storms (100-yr) plot higher. Chance in any year = 1 ÷ return period.

notes.title: Lightning
notes.html:
Ice and graupel collide in the cloud. Smaller, lighter ice rises with positive charge. Heavier graupel falls with negative charge. The cloud base is mostly negative. The ground below turns positive.

TypePath
Cloud-to-groundCloud to the surface
IntracloudInside one cloud
Cloud-to-cloudBetween two clouds
Cloud-to-airCloud into clear air

Lightning detection systems locate strikes using sensors across a network (they time the signal at each sensor).

Miles = seconds between flash and thunder ÷ 5

notes.title: Severe thunderstorms
notes.html:
NWS "severe": hail ≥ 1 inch, wind ≥ 58 mph, or a tornado.

TypeKey trait
Single-cellOne short-lived cell
MulticellCluster or line at different stages
SupercellOne long-lived storm with a rotating updraft (mesocyclone). Makes the strongest tornadoes
MCCLarge round long-lived cluster

Life cycle: cumulus (updraft only) → mature (updraft + downdraft, worst weather) → dissipating (downdraft only).

notes.title: Winds from storms
notes.html:
Straight-line winds = damage not from rotation. Damage is spread out in one direction.

TermMeaning
DowndraftSinking air
DownburstDowndraft that hits the ground and spreads out
MicroburstDownburst under 4 km wide. Brief, intense
MacroburstDownburst 4 km or wider. Longer lasting
Gust frontLeading edge of cool outflow
Squall lineOrganized line of storms
DerechoLong-lived, widespread windstorm. Track of hundreds of miles
Downslope windAir accelerating down a mountain slope

On radar: bow echo (derecho/damaging wind), fine line (gust front), bowing segment on a squall line.

notes.title: Tornadoes, scales, radar
notes.html:
Tornado = violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud base. Waterspout = same over water. Peak: late afternoon, spring, Plains and Southeast.

EF scale3-second gust
EF065–85 mph
EF186–110 mph
EF2111–135 mph
EF3136–165 mph
EF4166–200 mph
EF5over 200 mph
F scale = before 1 Feb 2007. EF scale = on or after. Both rate DAMAGE, not measured wind.
SignatureMeans
Hook echoRain/debris wrapping a mesocyclone (reflectivity)
TVSTight inbound-outbound velocity pair = intense rotation
Debris ballLow CC inside the hook = debris in the air
Bow echoStraight-line wind; may hide small tornadoes

notes.title: Hurricanes
notes.html:
Hurricane = typhoon = cyclone (same storm, different ocean). Needs warm water (about 26.5 °C or more), moisture, low shear, and distance from the equator.

Life cycle: Invest → Depression (under 39 mph) → Tropical Storm (39–73) → Hurricane (74+) → Major (Cat 3+).

Saffir-SimpsonSustained wind
Cat 174–95 mph
Cat 296–110 mph
Cat 3111–129 mph (major)
Cat 4130–156 mph (major)
Cat 5157+ mph (major)

Parts: eye (calm, 20–40 mi), eyewall (worst winds and rain), spiral bands (can spawn tornadoes).

Storm surge = water pushed onshore. Biggest with strong wind, large size, slow movement, and shallow, funnel-shaped coasts. Often the deadliest hazard.

Land cuts off the heat source, so storms weaken. Shear and dry air weaken them. El Niño tends to raise shear in the Atlantic and quiet it.

Atlantic season: June 1 – Nov 30.

notes.title: Severe winter storms
notes.html:
StormKey facts
BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours
Nor'easterStrong East Coast storm; northeast winds; snow, coastal flooding, wind
Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
Ice stormFreezing rain builds up ice. ¼ inch can bring down lines
A blizzard does not need new snow. Wind can blow old snow.

notes.title: Hazards and safety
notes.html:
StormMain hazard
TornadoViolent wind, debris
HurricaneStorm surge, wind, inland flooding
Severe thunderstormHail, wind, lightning
Flash floodRapid water rise
LightningDirect strike, fires
Winter stormSnow/ice load, low visibility, cold
Drought/heatWater shortage, heat illness
AlertMeans
WatchConditions favorable. Get ready
WarningHappening or about to. Act now
AdvisoryLess serious but still disruptive

Actions: tornado = lowest floor, interior room, no windows. Hurricane = follow evacuation orders. Flash flood = go high, never drive through water. Lightning = indoors or hard-topped car. Generators outside only (carbon monoxide).

Reliable sources: weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov (storms), nhc.noaa.gov (tropics).

written: A radar velocity image shows a bright inbound patch right next to a bright outbound patch inside a hook echo. A low correlation coefficient spot sits at the tip of the hook. What is happening and what should be issued?

A tornado is likely on the ground (tornadic vortex signature) and lofting debris (debris ball). The NWS should issue a Tornado Warning and people should shelter in an interior room on the lowest floor.
Explain why a hurricane's storm surge is often more deadly than its wind.

Surge pushes a wall of ocean water inland. Water is heavy and drowns people, destroys buildings, and floods large low areas quickly. Wind damage covers a smaller zone, and surge height depends on size, speed, wind and coast shape.
A town reports sustained 40 mph winds, heavy blowing snow, and 1/8 mile visibility for 4 hours with no new snowfall. Is it a blizzard? Explain.
Yes. Wind of at least 35 mph, snow in the air (blowing snow counts), visibility under ¼ mile, all for at least 3 hours. New snow is not required.
Describe the three ingredients that must come together for a supercell-producing environment.

Instability (CAPE) plus moisture to fuel the updraft, a lifting trigger such as a front, dryline or terrain, and strong wind shear, especially with direction change, to organize and rotate the updraft.
An observer counts 20 seconds between a flash and the thunder. How far away is the strike and what should they do?
About 4 miles (20 ÷ 5). Lightning can strike miles from the storm. Go indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle now.

Decode a 4-line METAR set. Make a table: station, time, wind (with gusts), visibility, weather, clouds with heights, temperature, dew point, altimeter.
Given reflectivity, velocity and correlation coefficient images, name the signature (hook, TVS, debris ball, bow echo, fine line), the hazard, and the NWS product you would expect.
Station 4: Read a sounding or hodograph
Mark where temperature and dew point nearly touch, any inversion, and the strongest shear layer. State if storms are likely to be strong and why. (Skew-T for States/Nationals.)
Given wind or damage data and a date, rate it with Fujita/EF or Saffir-Simpson and state which scale applies and why.
Given a data packet for a historic event, identify the storm type, three clues, the main hazard, and the safety action.
safety: Use only reliable sources: weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov, nhc.noaa.gov.
During real watches or warnings, follow official instructions, not this app.
Never chase storms or drive through flood water for practice.

sol: From your notes · Hurricanes: Life cycle: Invest → Depression (under 39 mph) → Tropical Storm (39–73) → Hurricane (74+) → Major (Cat 3+).

questions.q: Lake-effect snow occurs when…
o: Cold air crosses warmer lake water
sol: Moisture and heat from the lake make snow bands.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
questions.w: Moisture and heat from the lake make snow bands.

questions.q: Which is more dangerous: wind chill below 0°F or 32°F?
sol: Colder wind chills freeze skin faster.
questions.w: Colder wind chills freeze skin faster.

questions.q: A winter storm watch means…
Where is the safest place during a severe thunderstorm?
If caught outside in lightning with no shelter, you should…
o: Avoid being the tallest object; crouch low and keep feet together
sol: Minimize contact with the ground; get to shelter ASAP.
questions.w: Minimize contact with the ground; get to shelter ASAP.

questions.q: A NOAA Weather Radio is useful because it…
o: Sends alerts even if the power or phone fails

questions.q: Which source is best for official severe-weather alerts?
A flood watch means flooding is…
The Joplin tornado (2011) was rated…
Hurricane Katrina's largest losses came from…
The Dust Bowl was mostly caused by…
Which tool measures how hot or cold the air is?
sol: Common units are degrees Fahrenheit (°F) and degrees Celsius (°C).
questions.w: Common units are degrees Fahrenheit (°F) and degrees Celsius (°C).

questions.q: Which tool shows the direction the wind is blowing from?
sol: A wind vane has a tail that swings around.
The pointer faces into the wind, so it shows where the wind comes FROM.
questions.w: The pointer faces into the wind, so it shows where the wind comes FROM.

questions.q: Which tool measures how fast the wind is blowing?
sol: The faster they spin, the faster the wind. The tool is an anemometer.
questions.w: The faster they spin, the faster the wind. The tool is an anemometer.

questions.q: Which tool measures how much rain has fallen?
sol: A rain gauge is a tube that catches rain.
You read how deep the water is.
questions.w: You read how deep the water is.

questions.q: Which tool measures air pressure?
sol: Air has weight, and a barometer measures how hard it pushes.
The name comes from the Greek word baros, meaning weight.
questions.w: The name comes from the Greek word baros, meaning weight.

questions.q: Which tool measures how much water vapor is in the air?
A wind vane points toward the west. Which direction is the wind coming from?
sol: Wind is named for where it comes FROM.
The vane points into the wind, so this is a west wind.
questions.w: The vane points into the wind, so this is a west wind.

questions.q: The instrument package carried up by a weather balloon is called a…
sol: The balloon lifts a small box of sensors.
The box (a radiosonde) measures temperature, pressure and humidity and radios the data down.
questions.w: The box (a radiosonde) measures temperature, pressure and humidity and radios the data down.

questions.q: Cloud photos taken from space come from a weather…
sol: Satellites orbit Earth and take pictures of clouds.
They help forecasters see storms over oceans where there are few stations.
questions.w: They help forecasters see storms over oceans where there are few stations.

questions.q: A rain gauge collects 2.5 cm of rain on Monday and 1.5 cm on Tuesday. How many centimeters of rain is that in all?
A thermometer reads 20 °C in the morning and 28 °C in the afternoon. By how many degrees did it rise?
What is the word for the layer of gases that surrounds Earth?
sol: Meteorology is the study of the atmosphere.
questions.w: Meteorology is the study of the atmosphere.

questions.q: Convert 25 °C to degrees Fahrenheit. (°F = 9/5 × °C + 32)
Convert 50 °F to degrees Celsius. (°C = 5/9 × (°F − 32))
Convert 20 °C to kelvins. (K = °C + 273)
sol: 20 °C is 293 K. Kelvin has no negative values.
questions.w: 20 °C is 293 K. Kelvin has no negative values.

questions.q: A wind of 20 knots is about how many mph? (1 knot ≈ 1.15 mph)
A rain gauge has a narrow measuring tube with one-tenth the area of its funnel, so the water is 10 times deeper in the tube. The tube shows 0.50 cm of water. How many cm of rain actually fell?
sol: The tube makes depth 10 times larger, so divide the reading by 10.

questions.q: What does the Z in a time such as 12Z stand for?
sol: Weather data worldwide uses one clock so reports line up.
Z means Zulu time, which is the same as UTC.
questions.w: Z means Zulu time, which is the same as UTC.

questions.q: Radiosondes are launched at the same two times each day around the world. Which two UTC times?
sol: Launches are timed so every station reports at once.

questions.q: Which kind of satellite stays above one point on the equator: geostationary or polar-orbiting?
sol: A geostationary satellite orbits at the same rate Earth turns.
So it hovers over one spot and can watch the same area all the time.
questions.w: So it hovers over one spot and can watch the same area all the time.

questions.q: What instrument uses a laser or light beam to measure the height of the cloud base?
sol: Ceilo means ceiling, the height of the lowest cloud layer.

questions.q: A storm center reads 28.50 inches of mercury. Convert to hectopascals. (1 inHg ≈ 33.86 hPa)
Doppler radar measures the motion of raindrops along the radar beam. What is this speed called?
sol: Doppler radar sees whether drops move toward or away from the radar.
That motion along the beam is the radial velocity.
questions.w: That motion along the beam is the radial velocity.

questions.q: A barometer reading that falls quickly over a few hours usually means the weather is about to get…
sol: Falling pressure means a low-pressure system is approaching.
Lows bring clouds, wind and precipitation.
questions.w: Lows bring clouds, wind and precipitation.

questions.q: On a weather map, what does a large letter H mean?
sol: H marks a center of high pressure.
High pressure usually brings clear, calm weather.
questions.w: High pressure usually brings clear, calm weather.

questions.q: On a weather map, what does a large letter L mean?
sol: L marks a center of low pressure.
Low pressure usually brings clouds and storms.
questions.w: Low pressure usually brings clouds and storms.

questions.q: Lines on a weather map that connect places with equal air pressure are called…
sol: Iso means equal and bar means pressure.

questions.q: Lines on a weather map that connect places with equal temperature are called…
sol: Iso means equal and therm means heat.

questions.q: A blue line with triangles on a weather map shows which kind of front?
sol: Blue lines with triangles are cold fronts.
questions.w: Blue lines with triangles are cold fronts.

questions.q: A red line with half-circles on a weather map shows which kind of front?
sol: Red lines with half-circles are warm fronts.
questions.w: Red lines with half-circles are warm fronts.

questions.q: On a station model, a completely filled-in circle means the sky is…
sol: The circle shows how much of the sky is covered by cloud.
A filled circle means all of it: overcast.
questions.w: A filled circle means all of it: overcast.

questions.q: On a station model, an empty circle means the sky is…
sol: An empty circle means no cloud cover.

questions.q: On a map, 1 cm stands for 50 km. Two cities are 4 cm apart on the map. How many kilometers apart are they?
In the Northern Hemisphere, winds around a low-pressure center spin clockwise or counterclockwise?
sol: Winds spiral in toward a low and turn because Earth spins.
In the Northern Hemisphere that turn is counterclockwise.
questions.w: In the Northern Hemisphere that turn is counterclockwise.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds around a high-pressure center spin clockwise or counterclockwise?
sol: Highs spin the opposite way from lows.
In the Northern Hemisphere highs spin clockwise.
questions.w: In the Northern Hemisphere highs spin clockwise.

questions.q: A station model shows the pressure code 132. Add a leading 10 and put a decimal before the last digit. What is the pressure in hPa?
sol: For codes starting with 0, 1 or 2, put 10 in front.

questions.q: A station model shows the pressure code 987. For codes starting with 5 to 9, put a 9 in front and a decimal before the last digit. What is the pressure in hPa?
sol: The code starts with 9, so put a 9 in front: 9987.
Place the decimal before the last digit: 998.7 hPa.
questions.w: Place the decimal before the last digit: 998.7 hPa.

questions.q: A wind barb has one long barb and one short barb. What is the wind speed in knots? (long = 10, short = 5)
A wind barb has one flag (pennant, 50 knots) and two long barbs (10 knots each). What is the wind speed in knots?
A METAR reports wind 29008KT. From what direction, in degrees, is the wind blowing?
sol: The first three digits are the direction wind comes from.
290° is a wind from the west-northwest.
questions.w: 290° is a wind from the west-northwest.

questions.q: In a METAR, the group 18/09 gives temperature and dew point in °C. Which number is the dew point?
sol: Temperature comes first, then dew point.
The dew point is 09 °C, so the air is 9 °C from saturation.
questions.w: The dew point is 09 °C, so the air is 9 °C from saturation.

questions.q: On a surface map, are winds stronger where isobars are close together or far apart?
sol: Close isobars mean pressure changes quickly over a short distance.
A big pressure change over a short distance drives stronger wind.
questions.w: A big pressure change over a short distance drives stronger wind.

questions.q: A station model has its wind staff pointing toward the northwest. The wind is blowing FROM the northwest. Drag the pointer to that direction.
sol: The staff points toward where the wind comes from.

questions.q: The wind is blowing FROM the southeast. Drag the pointer to the direction the wind comes from.
sol: Southeast lies halfway between east (90°) and south (180°).

questions.q: On a weather map, two stations are 2.5 cm apart and 1 cm equals 120 km. How far apart are the stations?
sol: Multiply the map distance by the scale: 2.5 × 120.

questions.q: A stationary front is drawn with alternating red half-circles and blue triangles on opposite sides. What does the front do?
sol: The boundary stays nearly in place.
questions.w: The boundary stays nearly in place.

questions.q: Near the ground, temperature usually gets warmer or cooler as you climb higher in the atmosphere?
sol: Higher up, the air is thinner and farther from the warm ground.
In the troposphere the temperature falls with height.
questions.w: In the troposphere the temperature falls with height.

questions.q: What is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, where almost all weather happens?
sol: Tropo means to turn or mix.
The troposphere is the layer we live in.
questions.w: The troposphere is the layer we live in.

questions.q: A rising bubble of air is called an air…
sol: Forecasters imagine a small bubble of air.
They call it a parcel and follow it as it rises.
questions.w: They call it a parcel and follow it as it rises.

questions.q: Air pressure gets higher or lower as you climb up a mountain?
sol: There is less air above you pressing down.

questions.q: When rising air cools enough, water vapor turns into tiny droplets. This change is called…
A graph of temperature and moisture at different heights, made from a weather balloon, is called a…
sol: The balloon measures as it climbs.
The record of those measurements is called a sounding.
questions.w: The record of those measurements is called a sounding.

questions.q: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 10 °C per kilometer. A dry parcel at 25 °C rises 2 km. What is its new temperature?
A saturated parcel cools about 6 °C per km as it rises. How many degrees does it cool in 3 km?
Estimate the lifting condensation level (cloud base) with 125 m × (T − Td). The surface temperature is 30 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. How high is the cloud base?
A layer where temperature increases with height is called a(n)…
sol: When it warms with height instead, that is an inversion.
From your notes · Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE: A layer where temperature rises with height is an inversion (very stable, a "cap").
questions.w: When it warms with height instead, that is an inversion.

questions.q: What does CAPE stand for?
sol: CAPE measures the energy stored for rising air.

questions.q: CAPE is measured in joules per what?
sol: It is energy per mass of air.

questions.q: Larger CAPE means a stronger or weaker possible updraft?
sol: CAPE is the energy that can lift a parcel.

questions.q: A warm layer above the ground that stops rising air from reaching high levels is called a…
sol: If the cap breaks, storms can explode.
questions.w: If the cap breaks, storms can explode.

questions.q: On a sounding, the temperature is 20 °C at the surface and 4 °C at 2 km. What is the average lapse rate in °C per km?
The boundary between two different air masses is called a…
sol: Air masses have different temperature and moisture.
Where they meet is a front.
questions.w: Where they meet is a front.

questions.q: A large body of air with about the same temperature and moisture everywhere is an air…
sol: It forms over one kind of region for days.
This is called an air mass.
questions.w: This is called an air mass.

questions.q: Which is denser, warm air or cold air?
sol: Cold air has molecules packed closer.
Cold air is denser, so it sinks under warm air.
questions.w: Cold air is denser, so it sinks under warm air.

questions.q: A fast river of wind high in the sky is called the…
sol: It is a narrow band of strong winds.
It steers storms across the country.
questions.w: It steers storms across the country.

questions.q: Across the United States the jet stream mostly flows from which direction to which?
sol: Most of the winds above the middle latitudes blow from the west.
So the jet stream flows west to east.
questions.w: So the jet stream flows west to east.

questions.q: A cold front arrives and cool air replaces warm air. What usually happens to the temperature?
sol: Cold air is replacing warm air.

questions.q: Wind shear means the wind changes with…
sol: Shear is a change in wind speed or direction.
It is usually measured between two heights.
questions.w: It is usually measured between two heights.

questions.q: The wind is 15 knots from the south at the surface and 55 knots from the south at 6 km. What is the wind speed shear in knots?
A dryline separates moist air from what kind of air?
sol: The dryline marks a sharp drop in dew point.
Moist Gulf air is on one side and dry desert air on the other.
questions.w: Moist Gulf air is on one side and dry desert air on the other.

questions.q: A low-level jet is strongest at what time of day?
sol: After sunset the surface layer decouples from the winds above.
Winds a few hundred meters up speed up, especially at night.
questions.w: Winds a few hundred meters up speed up, especially at night.

questions.q: Does strong wind shear tend to organize thunderstorms (such as supercells) or tear them apart?
sol: Moderate to strong shear tilts the updraft.
Rain falls away from the updraft, so the storm lasts longer.
questions.w: Rain falls away from the updraft, so the storm lasts longer.

questions.q: A warm front moves in. What does warm air do as it overruns the cooler air ahead?
sol: It rides up over the cold air, making broad cloud layers.
questions.w: It rides up over the cold air, making broad cloud layers.

questions.q: The jet stream at 300 hPa is blowing FROM the west-southwest. Drag the pointer to that direction.
What is the name for puffy, cotton-like clouds with flat bottoms?
What is the name for thin, wispy clouds high in the sky made of ice crystals?
sol: Cirrus means a curl of hair.
These are the highest wispy clouds.
questions.w: These are the highest wispy clouds.

questions.q: What is the name for a flat, gray layer of cloud that covers the sky like a blanket?
Which cloud makes thunderstorms?
sol: It grows tall with strong updrafts.
Cumulo means heap, nimbus means rain: a rain heap.
questions.w: Cumulo means heap, nimbus means rain: a rain heap.

questions.q: The word nimbus on a cloud name means the cloud brings…
sol: Nimbus is Latin for rain cloud.

questions.q: What do we call a cloud that touches the ground?
sol: A cloud at ground level is fog.
It forms the same way as other clouds.
questions.w: It forms the same way as other clouds.

questions.q: The flat, spreading top of a thunderstorm is called an…
sol: Rising air hits a stable layer near the top of the troposphere.
It spreads sideways in the shape of an anvil.
questions.w: It spreads sideways in the shape of an anvil.

questions.q: Which thunderstorm cloud has pouch-like bulges hanging from the underside of the anvil?
sol: Sinking pockets of air form pouches.

questions.q: A long, low roll of cloud along the leading edge of a thunderstorm's cool outflow is called a(n)…
sol: Cool air from the storm pushes warm air up.
A shelf cloud forms on the gust front.
From your notes · Winds from storms: Gust frontLeading edge of cool outflow
questions.w: A shelf cloud forms on the gust front.

questions.q: A lowered, rotating cloud base beneath a supercell's updraft is called a…
sol: The wall cloud forms under the main updraft.

questions.q: A strong thunderstorm top reaches the tropopause at about 11 km. How many meters is that?
Put the cloud types in order from the lowest to the highest base height.
sol: Cumulus come next, altocumulus are mid-level, cirrus are highest.
questions.w: Cumulus come next, altocumulus are mid-level, cirrus are highest.

questions.q: Match each cloud feature to what it tells you.
pairs: Top of a thunderstorm spreading out
Rotating lowered base under a supercell
Gust front pushing warm air up
sol: Each feature has a typical position in a storm.
Learn them as a set when you read storm photos.
questions.w: Learn them as a set when you read storm photos.

questions.q: A long period with much less rain than normal is called a…
What should you drink more of during a heat wave?
sol: Your body loses water by sweating.
Drink water before you feel thirsty.
questions.w: Drink water before you feel thirsty.

questions.q: Should you ever leave a child or pet in a parked car on a hot day?
sol: A parked car heats up very fast, even with windows cracked.
Never leave a child or pet in a car.
questions.w: Never leave a child or pet in a car.

questions.q: The condition when the body gets too hot and sweating is not enough is called heat…
sol: Heat exhaustion is the earlier stage.
Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911.
questions.w: Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911.

questions.q: A town normally gets 40 mm of rain in a month but got only 10 mm. What percent of the normal rainfall fell?
The heat index makes 35 °C with high humidity feel hotter. If it feels like 41 °C, how many degrees hotter than the air temperature does it feel?
Why does high humidity make hot weather feel hotter?
sol: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates.
Humid air holds more water, so sweat evaporates slowly and cooling is weaker.
questions.w: Humid air holds more water, so sweat evaporates slowly and cooling is weaker.

questions.q: A heat dome is a strong area of what kind of pressure that traps hot air?
sol: Sinking air under a strong high heats up and clouds clear.
The air acts like a lid over the region.
questions.w: The air acts like a lid over the region.

questions.q: Which is the main reason a drought can become a wildfire problem: dry plants or heavy clouds?
sol: A spark can start a fire that spreads quickly.
questions.w: A spark can start a fire that spreads quickly.

questions.q: Overnight temperatures stay high during a heat wave. Why is this dangerous?
sol: The body needs a cool period to recover.
Warm nights add stress, especially for older adults.
questions.w: Warm nights add stress, especially for older adults.

questions.q: Rain falls at 5 mm per hour. Using light < 2.5, moderate 2.5 to 7.6, heavy > 7.6 mm/hr, how would you describe it?
A snowfall has a 10:1 snow-to-liquid ratio. How many cm of snow fall when the liquid equivalent is 5 cm?
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail is called…
A sudden, quick rise of water in a stream or on land after heavy rain is a…
sol: It can happen within minutes to hours.

questions.q: If you see water covering a road, what should you do?
sol: Just 15 to 30 cm of moving water can carry a car away.

questions.q: Which freezes into balls of ice during strong thunderstorms: rain or hail?
sol: Raindrops are lifted high and freeze in layers.
questions.w: Raindrops are lifted high and freeze in layers.

questions.q: A storm drops 12 mm of rain per hour for 4 hours. How many millimeters of rain is that in total?
Convert 2.54 cm of rain to inches. (1 in = 2.54 cm)
A rain gauge records 3 inches of rain in 6 hours. What is the average rate in inches per hour?
A watch vs. a warning: which one means flooding is already happening or imminent?
sol: A watch means conditions are favorable.
A warning means it is happening or about to happen.
questions.w: A warning means it is happening or about to happen.

questions.q: Why do flash floods happen faster in cities?
sol: Pavement and roofs do not let water soak in.
Water runs off quickly into streets and streams.
questions.w: Water runs off quickly into streets and streams.

questions.q: The sound you hear after a lightning flash is called…
sol: Lightning heats the air very fast.

questions.q: Which travels faster, light or sound?
sol: Light is almost instant for our purposes.
So you see lightning before you hear thunder.
questions.w: So you see lightning before you hear thunder.

questions.q: If you can hear thunder, are you close enough to be struck by lightning?
sol: Thunder can be heard about 10 miles away.
Lightning can strike that far from the storm: when thunder roars, go indoors.
questions.w: Lightning can strike that far from the storm: when thunder roars, go indoors.

questions.q: Where is the safest place during a lightning storm?
sol: A hard-topped car is the next best.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Lightning = indoors or hard-topped car.
questions.w: A hard-topped car is the next best.

questions.q: Should you stand under a lone tree during a thunderstorm?
Sound travels about 340 m/s. You hear thunder 6 seconds after a flash. About how far away is the lightning in meters?
A rough rule: divide the seconds between flash and thunder by 3 to get kilometers. The delay is 12 seconds. How many kilometers away?
sol: The strike is about 4 km away.
questions.w: The strike is about 4 km away.

questions.q: Divide seconds by 5 to get miles. The delay is 15 seconds. How many miles away?
sol: The strike is about 3 miles away.
questions.w: The strike is about 3 miles away.

questions.q: The 30-30 rule says go indoors if flash-to-bang is 30 seconds or less. How long should you wait after the last thunder before going back out?
sol: Storms can still strike after they seem to pass.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
questions.w: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

questions.q: Heat lightning is just lightning from a storm that is too what?
sol: The storm is too far to hear thunder.
You see the flashes but thunder does not reach you.
questions.w: You see the flashes but thunder does not reach you.

questions.q: Cloud-to-ground lightning that starts at the top of the storm and travels down starts as a stepped…
sol: A faint channel of charge moves down in steps.
When it meets an upward streamer, the return stroke flashes.
questions.w: When it meets an upward streamer, the return stroke flashes.

questions.q: A thunderstorm is severe if it makes hail at least how many inches across?
sol: Severe hail starts at 1 inch, about the size of a quarter.

questions.q: What three ingredients make a thunderstorm: moisture, lift and what else?
sol: Moisture gives fuel, lift gets air started, instability keeps it rising.
The three are moisture, lift and instability.
questions.w: The three are moisture, lift and instability.

questions.q: Which thunderstorm stage has both updrafts and downdrafts: developing, mature or dissipating?
sol: The storm is strongest in the mature stage.
Rain falls and drags air down while updrafts continue.
questions.w: Rain falls and drags air down while updrafts continue.

questions.q: A thunderstorm that makes strong rotating updrafts and lasts for hours is called a…
sol: Supercells make most big tornadoes and large hail.
questions.w: Supercells make most big tornadoes and large hail.

questions.q: A thunderstorm is classified severe if wind gusts reach at least 58 mph. A gust of 50 mph is how many mph below that threshold?
The rotating updraft in a supercell is called a…
sol: A mesocyclone is the rotating updraft.
questions.w: A mesocyclone is the rotating updraft.

questions.q: A strong storm outflow of sinking air that spreads at the ground is called a…
sol: Rain-cooled air sinks fast and fans out.
This sudden wind is a downburst.
questions.w: This sudden wind is a downburst.

questions.q: Thunderstorms that form in a line are called a…
sol: A squall line often has damaging winds.
questions.w: A squall line often has damaging winds.

questions.q: A multicell storm keeps renewing itself by forming new cells where?
sol: The cool outflow lifts warm air at its edge.
New updrafts form along the gust front.
questions.w: New updrafts form along the gust front.

questions.q: To grow large hail you need a strong…
sol: Hail stones keep rising and freezing.
Stronger updrafts hold bigger stones aloft.
questions.w: Stronger updrafts hold bigger stones aloft.

questions.q: A derecho is a long-lived windstorm. Its damage swath must stretch at least how many miles?
sol: A derecho has a swath at least about 240 miles (400 km) long with gusts of at least 58 mph.

questions.q: Wind is air moving from high pressure toward what?
sol: Air flows from high to low pressure.
It tries to even out pressure.
questions.w: It tries to even out pressure.

questions.q: A wind from the north blows toward which direction?
sol: Wind is named for where it comes from.
North wind moves toward the south.
questions.w: North wind moves toward the south.

questions.q: A strong, straight-line wind from a thunderstorm can knock down trees. Is it a tornado?
sol: Straight-line wind blows in one direction, not rotating.
questions.w: Straight-line wind blows in one direction, not rotating.

questions.q: A wind gust measured at 40 knots. Convert to mph. (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph)
What word describes sudden, brief increases in wind speed?
A wind is reported as blowing FROM the northeast. Drag the pointer to that direction.
sol: Northeast lies halfway between north (0°) and east (90°).

questions.q: What is a rotating column of air touching the ground called?
sol: From your notes · Tornadoes, scales, radar: Tornado = violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud base.

questions.q: Where should you go in a house during a tornado warning?
sol: Get as low as you can and away from windows.
A basement or small interior room on the lowest floor.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Actions: tornado = lowest floor, interior room, no windows.
questions.w: A basement or small interior room on the lowest floor.

questions.q: A tornado watch means tornadoes are possible. A tornado warning means a tornado is…
sol: It has been seen or radar shows rotation.
questions.w: It has been seen or radar shows rotation.

questions.q: The scale used to rate tornadoes by damage is called the…
sol: It runs from EF0 to EF5.

questions.q: A tornado is rated EF2 with winds up to 135 mph. The EF1 maximum is 110 mph. How many mph higher is the EF2 maximum?
A radar image with a hook shape on the south side of a supercell is called a…
sol: The precipitation wraps around the rotation.

questions.q: On Doppler velocity radar, a tight pair of inbound and outbound winds next to each other shows…
sol: Green is toward the radar, red is away.
Side by side, they mean rotation.
From your notes · Tornadoes, scales, radar: TVSTight inbound-outbound velocity pair = intense rotation
questions.w: Side by side, they mean rotation.

questions.q: On radar, what is a debris ball (tornado debris signature) made of?
sol: Dust and objects lofted into the air.
Radar sees them as a signature.
questions.w: Radar sees them as a signature.

questions.q: EF3 begins at 136 mph. A tornado has winds 12 mph below that. What is its wind speed?
sol: 124 mph, which is in the EF2 range (111–135).
questions.w: 124 mph, which is in the EF2 range (111–135).

questions.q: What do we call a huge spinning storm over warm ocean water with winds of 74 mph or more?
What is the calm center of a hurricane called?
sol: The eye has light winds and often clear skies.
But the strongest winds are right around it, in the eyewall.
questions.w: But the strongest winds are right around it, in the eyewall.

questions.q: In what season are most Atlantic hurricanes formed: summer-fall or winter?
sol: The Atlantic season is June 1 to November 30.
questions.w: The Atlantic season is June 1 to November 30.

questions.q: A hurricane needs warm ocean water. About what temperature, in °C, is the minimum?
sol: Warm water supplies heat and moisture.

questions.q: The rising mound of ocean water pushed onto shore by a hurricane is the storm…
sol: It is the deadliest hurricane hazard.

questions.q: A tropical storm has winds of 65 mph. How many mph more are needed to be a hurricane (74 mph)?
Which Saffir-Simpson category begins at 111 mph and is called a major hurricane?
sol: From your notes · Hurricanes: Life cycle: Invest → Depression (under 39 mph) → Tropical Storm (39–73) → Hurricane (74+) → Major (Cat 3+).

questions.q: What category is a hurricane with winds of 100 mph? (Cat 1: 74–95, Cat 2: 96–110, Cat 3: 111–129)
Which side of a Northern Hemisphere hurricane moving north has the strongest winds: right or left?
sol: Storm motion adds to the wind speed on one side.

questions.q: How does a hurricane weaken when it moves over land: it loses its supply of…?
sol: Warm ocean water is the fuel.
Over land, friction also slows the wind.
questions.w: Over land, friction also slows the wind.

questions.q: Is the eyewall or the outer rain band where the strongest winds usually are?
sol: It holds the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
questions.w: It holds the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

questions.q: Which wintry precipitation builds up the heaviest ice on power lines: sleet or freezing rain?
sol: Freezing rain freezes on contact and coats lines.
Sleet bounces and does not coat them.
questions.w: Sleet bounces and does not coat them.

questions.q: Frozen raindrops that bounce off the ground as small ice pellets are…
sol: Rain freezes as it falls through a cold layer.

questions.q: Rain that freezes when it touches the ground and coats everything with ice is…
sol: Drops are liquid until they touch cold surfaces.
Freezing rain makes roads very slippery.
questions.w: Freezing rain makes roads very slippery.

questions.q: A winter storm with strong winds and lots of blowing snow, with low visibility, is a…
sol: It needs winds of at least 35 mph for 3 hours.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours

questions.q: What can make cold air feel even colder when the wind blows?
sol: Wind carries heat away from skin.

questions.q: Should you travel during a blizzard warning?
sol: Visibility can drop to near zero.
Stay home or off the road.
questions.w: Stay home or off the road.

questions.q: A blizzard requires sustained winds of at least 35 mph. A storm has 28 mph. How many mph short is it?
A snowfall is 24 cm. Assuming a 10:1 ratio, how many cm of liquid water does it contain?
For freezing rain, the temperature aloft is above 0 °C and at the ground is…
sol: A warm layer melts snow into rain.
Near the ground a thin cold layer refreezes the water on contact.

questions.w: Near the ground a thin cold layer refreezes the water on contact.

questions.q: A lake-effect snow forms when cold air moves across what?
sol: Warm water adds heat and moisture.
Snow bands fall on the downwind shores.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
questions.w: Snow bands fall on the downwind shores.

questions.q: A watch means be prepared. A warning means to…
sol: A warning means the hazard is happening or imminent.

questions.q: When the weather service says warning, should you act right away?
sol: Warning means danger is happening or imminent.

questions.q: What weather radio sounds a loud alarm to alert you of danger?
sol: It broadcasts alerts 24 hours a day.
A tone alert can wake you at night.
questions.w: A tone alert can wake you at night.

questions.q: A kit with water, food, flashlight and batteries for emergencies is an emergency…
sol: Keep it ready before a storm.

questions.q: Should you stay away from downed power lines?
In a hurricane evacuation, you should follow orders from…
sol: Follow their evacuation zones and routes.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Hurricane = follow evacuation orders.
questions.w: Follow their evacuation zones and routes.

Why should you never run a generator indoors or in a garage?

sol: It crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.

questions.q: Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused major flooding in which U.S. city?

sol: It remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.

Hurricane Katrina made landfall in 2005. How many years before 2026 was that?
Hurricane Sandy (2012) was unusual because it merged with what kind of system before landfall?
sol: Sandy turned and merged with a cold front.

questions.w: It became a large post-tropical storm.

questions.q: The 1993 'Storm of the Century' brought snow to which part of the U.S.?
